L70@P1: We explore offer choice in multi-issue negotiations, where parties
L71@P1: seek to settle two or more negotiable issues that usually differ in value
L72@P1: between parties. In such cases, negotiators often begin by making a
L73@P1: package offer, presenting positions on each issue simultaneously (Iklé,
L74@P1: 1964; Kelley, 1966; Pruitt, 1981). Building off the concept of package
L75@P1: offers, we define offer choice as Multiple Equivalent Simultaneous Offers
L76@P1: (MESOs for short). Multiple and simultaneous indicate that MESOs include a choice of two or more package offers to the recipient and
L77@P1: equivalence denotes that, although each offer presents a different set of
L78@P1: issue positions, they are of the same value to the offerer. Relative to a
L79@P1: single package-offer, we propose that MESOs as first offers will reduce
L80@P1: the negotiator dilemma for offerers, allowing them to claim and create
L81@P1: more favorable economic and relational outcomes. They will do so, we
L82@P1: argue, in part by reducing the recipients’ experience of their own negotiator dilemma.
L83@P1: 2. Choice-derived consequences of MESOs
L84@P1: The offer that recipients typically receive is seen as suboptimal in
L85@P1: meeting their interests. Although it is an attempt at a potential agreement, it is usually perceived as competitively biased, making it less
L86@P1: worthy of full consideration. In contrast, we propose that presenting
L87@P1: two or more first offers, relative to just one, can reduce the negotiator
L88@P1: dilemma for the recipient by allowing them to simultaneously consider
L89@P1: the offers as a sincere attempt at reaching agreement while also pursuing their own interests.
L90@P1: There are two ways we propose that MESOs will reduce the recipient’s
L91@P1: negotiator dilemma. First, recipients are likely to prefer the experience of
L92@P1: choice relative to no choice, because it increases their flexibility in
L93@P1: reaching an agreement. This preference for the provision of choice is a
L94@P1: concept with a long history in psychology (Brehm, 1956; see also Gilbert &
L95@P1: Ebert, 2002; Kirkebøen & Teigen, 2011), one carefully differentiated from
L96@P1: economic explanations (Shin & Ariely, 2004). People prefer having a
L97@P1: choice because it gives them a greater sense of flexibility (Brehm, 1956;
L98@P1: see also Gilbert & Ebert, 2002; Simonson, 1990; in pigeons, Catania,
L99@P1: 1975), where people feel capable of pursuing their own interests.
L100@P1: Choice resulting from MESOs is also likely to produce flexibility by
L101@P1: offering different ways to accommodate the recipients’ interests.
L102@P1: Because recipients are likely to feel a choice accommodates their own
L103@P1: interests, it will impact their perception of the offers, reducing perceptions of competitive bias. Precisely, we think it will lead to what we
L104@P1: call agreement sincerity, which we define as the recipient’s perception
L105@P1: that the offer is a genuine and legitimate attempt at reaching an
L106@P1: agreement:
L107@P1: Agreement Sincerity Hypothesis: Recipients will perceive greater
L108@P1: agreement sincerity after receiving MESOs than a single packageoffer.
L109@P1: Second, we propose that MESOs will objectively offer more economic value than a single package-offer. In a typical multi-issue negotiation, where negotiators differ in issue preferences (i.e., some issues
L110@P1: more valuable to one, but less to the other), offer choice has the benefit
L111@P1: of probabilistically increasing the first offer’s economic value to the
L112@P1: recipient. The more offers that are presented, the more likely that one of
L113@P1: those offers will match a recipient’s issue preferences better than a
L114@P1: single offer would alone and thus provide them with more economic
L115@P1: value. Given that recipients will seek to maximize their own value, a
L116@P1: core tenet of rational choice theory and the foundation of many prescriptive economic models (e.g., Grether & Plott, 1979), MESOs will be
L117@P1: economically more favorable to recipients than single-package offers:
L118@P1: Initial Recipient-Value Hypothesis: Recipients will receive
L119@P1: greater value from MESOs than a single package-offer.
L120@P1: In sum, although recipients typically confront suboptimal first offers, the choice produced by MESOs can reduce their experience of the
L121@P1: negotiator dilemma in two ways: a choice among offers increases perceptions of agreement sincerity and, separately, present a higher initial
L122@P1: value for the recipient. We propose that these two processes have different economic consequences for the agreements negotiators make and
L123@P1: for the negotiator relationship. We detail these hypotheses below.
L124@P1: 3. Economic gains from MESOs
L125@P1: We propose that MESOs will produce better economic outcomes for
L126@P1: offerers. The most straightforward route to doing so would occur if
L127@P1: MESOs led recipients to accept one of the offers. Although possible, a
L128@P1: first offer is rarely immediately accepted (e.g., Galinsky, Mussweiler, &
L129@P1: Medvec, 2002). However, we predict MESOs can still produce economic
L130@P1: gains by shaping the counteroffers recipients generate, and ultimately,
L131@P1: the final agreements they reach. First, we propose that MESOs will yield
L132@P1: greater offerer outcomes (i.e., the agreement’s overall value the offerer
L133@P1: individually gains) because MESOs increase the agreement sincerity of
L134@P1: the offers. Second, MESOs will produce greater joint outcome (i.e., the
L135@P1: agreement’s overall value that the offerer and recipient collectively
L136@P1: gain) because they increase initial recipient-value.

L138@P1: We propose that presenting a choice among first offers will yield
L139@P1: greater offerer outcomes than a single package-offer. We hypothesize
L140@P1: this benefit occurs because the agreement sincerity resulting from
L141@P1: MESOs increases the likelihood that the first offer will anchor recipients
L142@P1: (Tversky & Kahneman, 1974; Whyte & Sebenius, 1997; in negotiations,
L143@P1: see Galinsky, Ku, & Mussweiler, 2009). To reach agreement, negotiators
L144@P1: need to decide a reasonable value for a negotiated resource and offer
L145@P1: recipients often turn to positions in the first offer – anchors – to decide
L146@P1: what their counteroffer will be. As a result, recipients are anchored on
L147@P1: and insufficiently adjust from the first offer even though it is biased to

L149@P1: 2001; Galinsky, Leonardelli, Okhuysen, & Mussweiler, 2005; Tasa,

L154@P1: judgments that adjust more from the initial anchor value, whereas with
L155@P1: strong anchors, judgments remain closer to the initial anchor value

L162@P1: death for any person.

L173@P1: MESOs will increase the anchoring strength of first-offer by increasing
L174@P1: the perceived agreement sincerity of those offers. After receiving

L85: ### Abstract
L86: In negotiations, where several issues are under consideration and parties have different priorities among these issues, integrative agreements can be reached through ‘logrolling’: concessions on low priority issues in exchange for gains on higher priority issues. The present research focuses on the potential role of initial offers in the development of integrative agreements.
L87: We show first, that in a simulated competitive market the specific composition of initial offers influences the final agreements, beyond the effect predicted by their overall value. In order to obtain some insight into the judgmental processes that might play a role, we explore the way in which inexperienced negotiators presented with a hypothetical negotiation context evaluate and respond to logrolling versus distributive initial offers.
L88: Three hypotheses were tested: logrolling offers convey an implicit message of cooperation, logrolling offers promote understanding of the mutual interest structure of the task, and, finally, logrolling offers establish within-issue anchors. Results do not support the first two hypotheses: logrolling offers were not necessarily judged more attractive than distributive ones, and they did not seem to affect the deeply rooted fixed-pie assumption.
L89: However, initial offers did establish within-issue anchors: counter-offers were affected by the specific composition of the initial offers beyond the effect of their overall value. This anchoring process resulted in logrolling offers yielding a higher profit for their initiator, as well as higher combined profits for both parties. Copyright © 2002 John Wiley & Sons, Ltd.

L57: ## Abstract
L58: In this paper we review the literature on first offers in negotiations. We explore the determinants of who will make the first offer, how extreme that first offer will be, what effect the first offer has on the value of the final outcome, and how first offers influence post-negotiation evaluations. L61:  cite15†Registered:†authors.repec.org L62: ## Abstract
L63:  In this paper, we develop a typology of bargaining steps for multi-issue negotiations, which is derived from possible changes in single issues. By considering all combinations of such changes, we create a consistent classification of steps. This classification forms the basis of an empirical analysis of the impact of different types of bargaining steps on various outcome dimensions of negotiations.
L64: We perform an exploratory analysis based on an ex-post analysis of existing negotiation data, which was collected over several years using an Internet-based negotiation support system. Empirical results indicate a strong positive impact of log-rolling strategies and a negative impact of “hard” tactics like insistence on the chances of reaching an agreement. Contrary to expectations, hard tactics do not improve the efficiency of agreements.

# Negotiation¶

Not every price is final. When the buyer has Agency or Advertiser tier access, it can negotiate with the seller before committing to a booking. Negotiation sits between inventory research and order execution in the overall buyer workflow --- the agent has already identified what it wants to buy, and now works to get a better price before the deal is booked.

The buyer agent includes a pluggable negotiation module for multi-turn price negotiation with seller agents. You can run fully automatic negotiations or drive them step-by-step.

Tier Requirement

Only Agency and Advertiser tier buyers can negotiate. Public and Seat tier buyers cannot — the seller will reject negotiation attempts from those tiers.

## How It Works¶
    
    `sequenceDiagram
        participant Buyer as Buyer Agent
        participant Strategy as NegotiationStrategy
        participant Client as NegotiationClient
        participant Seller as Seller Agent
    
        Buyer->>Strategy: next_offer() → $20 CPM
        Buyer->>Client: start_negotiation($20)
        Client->>Seller: POST /api/v1/negotiations/messages {action: "counter", buyer_price: 20}
        Seller-->>Client: {seller_price: 32, action: "counter"}
        Client->>Strategy: should_accept($32)?
        Strategy-->>Client: No
        Client->>Strategy: should_walk_away($32)?
        Strategy-->>Client: No
        Client->>Strategy: next_offer($32) → $22
        Client->>Seller: POST /api/v1/negotiations/messages {action: "counter", buyer_price: 22}
        Seller-->>Client: {seller_price: 28, action: "counter"}
        Client->>Strategy: should_accept($28)?
        Strategy-->>Client: Yes (≤ max_cpm $30)
        Client->>Seller: POST /api/v1/negotiations/messages {action: "accept"}
        Seller-->>Client: Deal confirmed at $28
    `

## Strategies¶

Negotiation behavior is controlled by a strategy — a pluggable class that decides when to accept, what to counter, and when to walk away.

### SimpleThresholdStrategy (v1)¶

The production-ready strategy. Uses fixed thresholds with linear concession steps.
    
    `from ad_buyer.negotiation.strategies.simple_threshold import SimpleThresholdStrategy
    
    strategy = SimpleThresholdStrategy(
        target_cpm=20.0,       # Ideal price — our opening offer
        max_cpm=30.0,          # Absolute ceiling — accept anything at or below
        concession_step=2.0,   # Concede $2 per round
        max_rounds=5,          # Walk away after 5 rounds
    )
    `

Decision logic:

Decision  | Rule
--- | ---
Accept  | Seller price ≤ `max_cpm`
Next offer  | Last offer + `concession_step` (capped at `max_cpm`)
Walk away  | Rounds exceeded `max_rounds` OR seller hasn't moved since last round

Behavior profiles:

Profile  | target_cpm  | max_cpm  | concession_step  | max_rounds  | Behavior
--- | --- | --- | --- | --- | ---
Conservative  | $15  | $20  | $1  | 3  | Tight budget, small concessions, quick exit
Balanced  | $20  | $30  | $2  | 5  | Moderate flexibility
Aggressive  | $15  | $35  | $5  | 10  | Wide range, big concessions, persistent

### AdaptiveStrategy¶

Adjusts concession behavior dynamically based on observed seller patterns --- if the seller is conceding aggressively, the buyer holds firm; if the seller holds firm, the buyer concedes faster to avoid stalemate.

Coming Soon

AdaptiveStrategy implements the same `NegotiationStrategy` interface and will be a drop-in replacement for `SimpleThresholdStrategy`.

### CompetitiveStrategy¶

Uses cross-seller intelligence to drive harder bargains when the buyer is shopping multiple sellers simultaneously, leveraging competing quotes as anchor points for negotiation.

Coming Soon

CompetitiveStrategy requires the Multi-Seller Orchestration capability to provide cross-seller context.

# Anatomy of a Defensible Score¶

A score you cannot walk by hand is not defensible — it is a rumour with a number attached. In Lodestar, our example agent for a regulated professional-services market, every buyer score is a pure function: the same inputs produce the same output, every time, with no hidden state and no call to a model in the hot path. This page walks the full computation with real numbers so you can reproduce it on paper.

## The three arithmetic steps¶

There are only three operations, and none of them is clever.

  1. Variable to layer. Each layer holds six variables, each scored 1-5. A layer score is the mean of its variables, multiplied by 20. That maps `[1,5]` onto `[20,100]`.
  2. Layers to composite. The buyer score is a weighted sum of three layer scores. The weights are fixed and declared: Need 0.40, Attractiveness 0.25, Winnability 0.35. They sum to 1.0, so the composite stays on the 0-100 scale.
  3. Composite to band. The composite is bucketed into a priority band by fixed thresholds.

PONYTAIL MODE ACTIVE — level: full

# Ponytail

You are a lazy senior developer. The best code is the code never written. You solve the whole problem with the least new code. End your reply with one or two lines: what you skipped or did not check, and any risk the user must know.

Active for the whole session until the user says "stop ponytail" or "normal mode". Switch level: `/ponytail lite|full|ultra`.

## Before you write

Read the task and the code it touches. List every place your change must reach: callers, tests, fixtures, config, exports. Check what your change could break for users: data it would destroy or expose, callers that stop working. That is scope. Extra features are not.

## The smallest complete change

Take the first option that fully works:

1. Does it need to exist? Skip features, options and flexibility nobody asked for, and name them in one line. A vague request ("build me X") gets the smallest version that does the core job.
2. Already in this codebase (a helper, component, service, pattern)? Use it the way the surrounding code does.
3. Standard library or a platform feature? Use it, unless the project has its own. A house component beats a native widget.
4. An installed dependency? Use it. Never add a dependency for a few lines.
5. Can it be one line a reader gets at a glance? One line.
6. Otherwise: the minimum code that works.

- Be lazy about the solution, never about the change itself: finish every part the task needs, including the callers, tests and fixtures your change breaks.
- No abstraction, wrapper, type conversion, option, config, boilerplate or "for later" code nobody asked for. Keep values in the form the platform already gives you. Deletion beats addition. Keep the structure the codebase already has: its layers, interfaces and conventions.
- The shortest working diff wins, once you know everything it must touch. A one-liner that needs decoding is not short.
- Comment only the why the code cannot show, in one line.
- Bug fix: before you edit, grep every caller of the function you touch, then fix the root cause once in the shared code.
- Code you move or merge keeps its error handling and validation.
- Between options of equal size, take the one that is correct on edge cases.
- Lazy code without its check is unfinished: new non-trivial logic (a branch, a loop, a parser, money or security, or a whole new script or app) leaves one small test or an assert-based self-check. Trivial changes need none.
- A shortcut with a known limit gets a code comment in this form: `shortcut: <the limit>, <when to upgrade>`.

Never cut: validation at trust boundaries, error handling that prevents data loss, security, accessibility, the calibration real hardware needs, anything the user asked for.

| Level | Behavior |
|-------|----------|
| **full** | The rules above. Default. |

# Taktika Buyer Agent

Taktika is a standalone procurement agent for the Tacto Negotiation Arena. It uses the arena API and
published total-cost model, then adds its own case research, offer planning, and conservative email
writer. By default, Python chooses the supplier, terms, acceptance, and walk-away. An optional
specialist council can propose bounded term changes and assess rejection risk; Python still validates
every proposed term sheet against the case rules and the best alternative.

All arena-facing Python code lives in this repository: the HTTP client, attachment reader, cost
calculator, session runner, research, and offer planner. Runtime dependencies are general-purpose
HTTP, PDF, spreadsheet, and environment-variable libraries; no negotiation starter package is
installed or imported.

## Install

Requires Python 3.12 and [uv](https://docs.astral.sh/uv/).

```bash
uv sync
cp .env.example .env
```

Set `ARENA_URL` and `ARENA_API_KEY` in `.env`. Keep that file private. The bundled research package
is in `data/`. Relative `ARENA_DATA` and `ARENA_RELEASE` paths resolve from this project directory,
even when you launch the CLI from elsewhere; if `ARENA_DATA` is missing or invalid, the agent falls
back to the bundled package.

## Run

```bash
uv run taktika me
uv run taktika cases --set practice
uv run taktika --verbose play case:P01 --record ./runs
uv run taktika run --set practice --parallel 8
uv run taktika run --set practice --limit 6 --parallel 1
uv run taktika analyze ./runs --replay
```

`play` and `run` automatically save a private JSON trace for each session and a timestamped result
summary under `./runs`. The console prints one consolidated score line. Pass `--record DIR` to use a
different directory. Traces include case data, supplier messages, planner research inputs, decisions,
and Arena results; keep them local. `analyze` reads these files without connecting to the Arena.
It reports recorded rejection forecasts against observed supplier replies; `--replay` compares
decisions with the current planner but does not simulate supplier responses or estimate a new score.

For the live final, start the runner before the first wave and leave it running:

```bash
uv run taktika run --set final --parallel 10
```

The runner uses the arena's replay and session machinery, including attachment extraction, API
retry handling, final wave deadlines, and safe case resumption. A practice run consumes the team's
practice quota.

## How the agent works

1. **Research:** joins same-part, same-unit purchase orders, RFQ quotes, should-cost estimates, and
   supplier scorecards. It also calculates cost-weighted market index changes and keeps only data
   IDs the case or local package can verify.
2. **Plan:** sets a target from the current purchase price and market movement, adjusts it for the
   category goal and same-part competitor quotes, and prices complete term sheets with the arena's
   cost function. Each supplier is compared with the best alternative excluding that supplier.
3. **Negotiate:** sends a staged concession curve and up to three concrete packages. Each package
   must satisfy every must-have and stay within the alternative's total cost. Valid standing offers
   are accepted once they meet target or reach their final round; otherwise the agent walks away
   after every supplier conversation is exhausted.
4. **Write:** produces a short, supplier-aware email. With no model configured, the built-in writer
   works without a paid API. If configured, an OpenAI-compatible model drafts prose only; messages
   containing numbers or commercial thresholds are rejected in favor of the built-in wording.

### Optional specialist council

Set `LLM_API_KEY`, `LLM_COUNCIL_ENABLED=true`, and `LLM_COUNCIL_MODEL=gpt-6-luna` to let independent
money, payment, delivery, quality, contract, market/index, relationship, and evidence/alternatives
specialists advise one rejection-risk specialist and one decision boss. Set the council model to
`gpt-4o` for that model instead. Only terms owned by the matching specialist are considered. The
boss can select at most three packages; Python rejects unsupported options, broken must-haves, and
offers beyond the current earned cost limit. Existing agreed offers and walk-away decisions stay
deterministic.

GPT-6 Luna is the default because this workflow makes several narrow model calls per decision and
OpenAI Docs positions Luna for focused, high-volume tasks. Current standard token rates are `$0.10`
input / `$0.50` output per million tokens for Luna versus `$2.50` / `$10` for GPT-4o. This is a cost
choice, not a measured quality win; compare both on the same practice cases before switching models
for real negotiations ([Luna](https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/models/gpt-6-luna),
[GPT-4o](https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/models/gpt-4o),
[pricing](https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/pricing)).

The rejection specialist separately estimates acceptance, counteroffer, and supplier walk-away
probabilities. It marks confidence as low, medium, or high; low-confidence, malformed, timed-out, or
over-budget advice falls back to the deterministic planner. Probabilities are not calibrated against
the small available negotiation history. The trace stores specialist findings, risk estimates,
the boss's reason, and council API cost. The council uses the existing safe email wording.

`LLM_API_BUDGET_USD` caps council API calls for one running process (default `$2`, hard maximum `$5`,
using the bundled published-rate estimates).
The process-wide ledger reserves the maximum request cost before each call and charges the full
reservation if usage is not returned. It covers council calls; keep one runner process active for
one negotiation batch.
Only GPT-6 Luna and GPT-4o have built-in budget rates. The council falls back if another model is
configured.

For optional model drafting, set `LLM_PROVIDER=openai-compatible`, `LLM_MODEL=gpt-6-luna`, and
`LLM_API_KEY` in `.env`; optionally set `LLM_BASE_URL` for another OpenAI-compatible endpoint.
Without a model API key, the built-in writer is used. The model does not choose terms or accept offers.

## MCP email tools

Taktika also exposes the Arena's supplier-email workflow as an MCP server over stdio. Start it from
the project directory after configuring `.env`:

```bash
uv run taktika-mcp
```

Register it with an MCP client using its project folder as the working directory. For clients that
use a JSON server configuration, the entry is:

```json
{
  "mcpServers": {
    "taktika-arena": {
      "command": "uv",
      "args": ["--directory", "/absolute/path/to/ai-agent-tacto", "run", "taktika-mcp"]
    }
  }
}
```

The server provides tools to list cases, start a negotiation, read supplier emails, ask Taktika to
draft its next email, send an email with up to three term sheets, and accept or walk away. Drafting
does not send anything; `send_negotiation_email` and `close_negotiation` submit actions to the Arena
when called. Starting a practice negotiation uses one case from the team's practice quota. These are
Arena negotiation emails, not a personal Gmail or Outlook inbox. For a retry after a timed-out MCP
call, pass the same `operation_id` to `start_negotiation`, `send_negotiation_email`, or
`close_negotiation`; use a new ID when intentionally repeating an operation. The operation journal
is stored under `TAKTIKA_STATE_DIR` or `~/.taktika-buyer-agent` and contains local request/result data.

## Data and attribution

The research files are provided by Tacto Technology GmbH under CC BY 4.0. Their attribution and
source licences are retained in [LICENSE-data](LICENSE-data) and [data/ATTRIBUTION.md](data/ATTRIBUTION.md).
The agent code is MIT licensed; see [LICENSE](LICENSE).
The research snapshot is synthetic company data with public market series, and should be refreshed
from the arena before a new event when updated data is available.

Taktika also exposes the Arena's supplier-email workflow as an MCP server over stdio. Start it from
the project directory after configuring `.env`:

```bash
uv run taktika-mcp
```

Register it with an MCP client using its project folder as the working directory. For clients that
use a JSON server configuration, the entry is:

```json
{
  "mcpServers": {
    "taktika-arena": {
      "command": "uv",
      "args": ["--directory", "/absolute/path/to/ai-agent-tacto", "run", "taktika-mcp"]
    }
  }
}
```

The server provides tools to list cases, start a negotiation, read supplier emails, ask Taktika to
draft its next email, send an email with up to three term sheets, and accept or walk away. Drafting
does not send anything; `send_negotiation_email` and `close_negotiation` submit actions to the Arena
when called. Starting a practice negotiation uses one case from the team's practice quota. These are
Arena negotiation emails, not a personal Gmail or Outlook inbox. For a retry after a timed-out MCP
call, pass the same `operation_id` to `start_negotiation`, `send_negotiation_email`, or
`close_negotiation`; use a new ID when intentionally repeating an operation. The operation journal
is stored under `TAKTIKA_STATE_DIR` or `~/.taktika-buyer-agent` and contains local request/result data.
